title: Ibn Waḥshiyya and the Riddles of the Ancient Scripts (Shawq al-mustahām)
otherNames: Kitāb Shawq al-mustahām fī maʿrifat rumūz al-aqlām (شوق المستهام في معرفة رموز الأقلام)
Ancient Alphabets and Hieroglyphic Characters Explained (Joseph Hammer's English title, London, 1806)
Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Waḥshiyya al-Nabaṭī (the usual modern form of the author's name)
'Ahmad Bin Abubekr Bin Wahshih' (the form on Hammer's 1806 title page, which turns the kunya Abū Bakr into a father's name)
aqlām, 'pens', i.e. scripts (Arabic word for these alphabets)
al-khawātim, 'the seals' (Arabic, for the related seal-signs of talismanic practice; not the title of this book)
family: Not a single alphabet. A book, ascribed to Ibn Waḥshiyya, that catalogues several dozen scripts: real scripts of earlier peoples, alphabets credited to Hermes and to the Greek sages, planetary alphabets, and Egyptian hieroglyphs given Arabic letter values. It belongs to the Arabic literature of aqlām, 'scripts', in which ring-ended alphabets of the 'sages' and the seven seal-signs (al-khawātim) carry on the charaktêres of late-antique magic.
summary: Shawq al-mustahām is an Arabic catalogue of 'ancient' alphabets. It is ascribed to Ibn Waḥshiyya, the Iraqi writer active about 900–930 who gave out the Nabatean Agriculture; Jaakko Hämeen-Anttila (2006) doubts that the Shawq is his. Beside scripts of real peoples, it gives alphabets credited to Hermes, to Greek sages and to the planets, and it presents Egyptian hieroglyphs as signs with Arabic letter values. Joseph Hammer printed the Arabic with an English version in London in 1806 as Ancient Alphabets and Hieroglyphic Characters Explained. Okasha El Daly (2005) argues that the book gets some hieroglyph sound values right and sees that some signs stand for ideas rather than sounds; that reading is disputed, and the decipherment of hieroglyphs is Champollion's work of 1822.

firstAttestation.author: ascribed to Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Waḥshiyya; authorship doubted (Hämeen-Anttila 2006)
firstAttestation.date: If the ascription holds, late 9th or early 10th century CE: Ibn Waḥshiyya's Nabatean Agriculture was dictated in 318 AH / 930–31 CE according to its transmitter (Hämeen-Anttila 2006). firstAttestation.place: Iraq is Ibn Waḥshiyya's milieu; where the Shawq itself was written is not known. Hammer's copy came, by his account as I recall it, from Cairo.

transmission.date: c. 900–930 CE (318 AH / 930–31 CE for the Nabatean Agriculture)
transmission.work: al-Filāḥa al-Nabaṭiyya (Nabatean Agriculture) and the other works under his name
transmission.author: Ibn Waḥshiyya; transmitted by his pupil Abū Ṭālib al-Zayyāt
transmission.what: Fixes the author's date. The Nabatean Agriculture presents itself as a translation of ancient 'Nabataean' (Aramaic, Iraqi) books. In Ibn Waḥshiyya, 'Nabataean' means the Aramaic-speaking country people of Iraq, not the Nabataeans of Petra. The Shawq claims to unlock the scripts of such ancient books. Sources: Hämeen-Anttila 2006; T. Fahd, 'Ibn Waḥshiyya', EI2 III (1971). Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: Ibn al-Nadīm
transmission.what: The Baghdad bookseller's catalogue has a notice of Ibn Waḥshiyya and his books (English: B. Dodge, The Fihrist of al-Nadīm, 1970). Its first discourse also surveys the scripts of the nations, the same ground the Shawq covers. I did not check whether the Fihrist names the Shawq. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Ancient Alphabets and Hieroglyphic Characters Explained; with an Account of the Egyptian Priests, their Classes, Initiation, and Sacrifices (London: W. Bulmer and Co.)
transmission.author: Joseph Hammer (from 1835 Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, 1774–1856), then in the Austrian diplomatic service
transmission.what: First printing. The Arabic text and its alphabets are given with an English version and offered to European readers as a key to the hieroglyphs, a live question since the Rosetta Stone reached London in 1802. Wording of the title and imprint follows my memory of the title page; check it against a scan. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: Jean-François Champollion
transmission.what: Context, not transmission. The decipherment that worked came from bilingual inscriptions and Coptic, not from this book. Any influence of Hammer's volume on Champollion is unproved (see claims). Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Egyptology: The Missing Millennium. Ancient Egypt in Medieval Arabic Writings (London: UCL Press; series Encounters with Ancient Egypt)
transmission.author: Okasha El Daly
transmission.what: Re-reads the Shawq's hieroglyph section, with other medieval Arabic writers on Egypt. He argues that Ibn Waḥshiyya got some sign values right and saw that some signs mark meaning rather than sound. The book revived the Shawq's reputation and drew popular claims that Arabs deciphered hieroglyphs before Champollion. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: Jaakko Hämeen-Anttila
transmission.what: The standard modern study of Ibn Waḥshiyya. It sorts the works under his name into those likely his and those doubtful, and it doubts the Shawq. The exact wording and page of his verdict were not checked in this run. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Ibn Waḥshiyya was a real author active in Iraq about 900–930. His Nabatean Agriculture was dictated in 318 AH / 930–31 CE.
claims.evidence: The transmitter's preface to the Nabatean Agriculture, as analysed by Hämeen-Anttila (2006); Fahd's EI2 article. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Shawq al-mustahām is by Ibn Waḥshiyya.
claims.evidence: The manuscripts and Hammer's edition carry his name. Hämeen-Anttila (2006) doubts it and treats it as one of the works later attached to his name; El Daly (2005) works with it as Ibn Waḥshiyya's. Give both views. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The book catalogues several dozen scripts: scripts of real peoples, alphabets credited to Hermes and to named Greek sages, planetary alphabets and Egyptian hieroglyphs with Arabic letter values.
claims.evidence: Contents of Hammer's 1806 edition as I recall them; the hieroglyph part is in Hammer's title. The exact number of alphabets and the order of the chapters were not checked, so give no count on the page. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The alphabets credited to Hermes, Plato, Pythagoras and the other sages are the scripts those men wrote in.
claims.evidence: This is the book's own frame. No such alphabet is found in any Greek source. They belong to the stock of ring-ended magical alphabets (aqlām of the sages) known from Arabic and other magical manuscripts. Arabic belief in an ancient Hermes as the first teacher of writing and the sciences is traced by van Bladel (2009). Report it as 'the book ascribes this alphabet to Hermes', never 'Hermes' alphabet'. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The book explains Egyptian hieroglyphs: it treats them as letters with Arabic values, with some signs standing for whole words or ideas.
claims.evidence: This is the book's claim, made in its hieroglyph section and in Hammer's title. That the book makes the claim is documented; that the claim is right is a separate question (next item). Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Ibn Waḥshiyya (partly) deciphered hieroglyphs: he got some sign values right and understood that some signs mark meaning (determinatives), centuries before Champollion.
claims.evidence: El Daly (2005) argues it, matching a number of the book's values with modern ones. Against: the authorship is doubted (Hämeen-Anttila 2006). The book's framework, one sign per Arabic letter, is wrong for Egyptian. Many of its 'hieroglyphs' are not attested Egyptian signs. A few right values can come from Coptic, which kept the old words, or from chance. And no Egyptian text is known to have been read with the book. The working decipherment is Champollion's (1822). Present it as El Daly's argument, with the objections. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began). I could not check how many values El Daly counts as right, or name a published review, so give neither.

claims.claim: Hammer found the manuscript in Cairo.
claims.evidence: Hammer's own account in the 1806 volume, as I recall it. He was in Egypt with the British and Ottoman forces in 1801. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Hammer's book helped Champollion decipher the hieroglyphs.
claims.evidence: The claim turns up in popular retellings. I know of no documentary evidence that the book shaped Champollion's method, and the 1822 Lettre rests on cartouches, the bilingual inscriptions and Coptic. At most it was one of the books in circulation. Do not print it as fact. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Arabic talismanic practice uses ring-ended 'scripts of the sages' (aqlām) and a fixed row of seven seal-signs, al-khawātim al-sabʿa. They are read as the Greatest Name of God and are described in a poem that opens 'three staffs set in a row after a seal'.
claims.evidence: The seven seals and their poem are in the corpus under al-Būnī's name (d. 622/1225 or 630/1232–3), whose printed Shams al-maʿārif al-kubrā is a much later compilation (Gardiner 2012; Coulon 2017; already stated in the Arabic hall). Seals and amulets carry the signs (Porter 2011). The poem's ascription varies; tradition gives it to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, which is legend. This is the setting the Shawq belongs to, not a claim about the Shawq itself. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The ring-ended Arabic aqlām and the seven seals descend from the charaktêres of Graeco-Egyptian magic.
claims.evidence: Scholars argue it from shared ring-ended forms and from the Jewish and Christian links between them (Bohak 2011; the charakteres sibling file). No unbroken line of manuscripts proves it sign by sign. Say 'scholars connect them'. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: Scripts of the ancient nations
letters.value: Arabic letters (each table is keyed to the Arabic alphabet; abjad order is likely but was not checked)
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. The book gives tables for the scripts of peoples, real and legendary: as I recall, Syriac, 'Nabataean' or Chaldaean, Hebrew, Greek, Coptic, South Arabian (musnad), Persian and Indian. Copied by Arabic scribes, the real scripts are often garbled. Show a facsimile crop from Hammer 1806 (public domain) beside the real script from the matching Scriptorium hall, so readers can see how far the copy has drifted. Do not redraw these from modern charts.
letters.note: 'formConfidence' grades the card's facts (that the book has this kind of table), not a drawing. The list of peoples is from memory; trim it to what the facsimile shows. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: The Hermetic alphabets
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. One or more alphabets the book ascribes to Hermes. Arabic tradition knew three Hermeses (van Bladel 2009), and the book may label its tables by them. As I recall, the forms are of the ring-ended magical kind: thin strokes ending in small circles. No letter-level description is given here. Draw only from a facsimile of the 1806 plates.
letters.note: Wording on the page: 'an alphabet the book ascribes to Hermes'. How many Hermetic tables there are, and under which Hermes, was not checked. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: The alphabets of the sages and philosophers
letters.translit: aqlām al-ḥukamāʾ, 'pens of the sages' (descriptive label)
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. Alphabets ascribed to named ancient philosophers and physicians in Arabic name-forms. Plato, Pythagoras, Socrates, Aristotle, Hippocrates and Asclepius are the kind of names I recall; check each one against the facsimile before printing. Many are ring-letter alphabets, close in style to the charaktêres. No letter-level description is given here.
letters.note: The heart of the 'aqlām of the sages' tradition. The ascriptions are the book's (legend). These sages are not known to have used any secret script. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: The planetary alphabets
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. As I recall, one alphabet for each of the seven planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon), for writing under that planet's rule. Expected to be ring-ended. No letter-level description is given here.
letters.note: No link to Agrippa's planetary seals and characters (De occulta philosophia II.22) or to his Hebrew-keyed alphabets (III.30) is known. Show them side by side only as a parallel, never as a source. Also check the facsimile for zodiacal alphabets (twelve signs), which I half-remember and could not confirm. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: The alphabet of the Kabbalists
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. The commissioning brief names an 'alphabet of the Kabbalists' in the book. I could not confirm the label, the Arabic behind Hammer's word, or the forms. Leave this unit out unless the facsimile shows it.
letters.note: If it exists, a label in an Arabic book is not evidence that Jewish kabbalists used the script; say so on the page. Compare the Hebrew-keyed ring-letter alphabets in the celestial, malachim and transitus-fluvii files. I have a faint, unconfirmed memory that the label may go with the Arabic qalfaṭīrī ring-script; do not print that. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: The tree alphabets
letters.translit: al-mushajjar, 'the tree-shaped' (term as I recall it)
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. As I recall, scripts built on an upright stem, with each letter told apart by the number and side of short branch strokes, a principle like Irish ogham and Norse cipher-runes. No letter-level description is given here, and the stem-and-branch principle must not be used to invent letters.
letters.note: The likeness to ogham has drawn 19th-century antiquarians and later fringe epigraphers to Hammer's tables. It shows a shared cipher principle, not a historical connection. Whether the term mushajjar is the book's own was not checked. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: Hieroglyphs read as letters
letters.value: Arabic letters (one or more hieroglyph-like signs for each letter)
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. The book's tables pair hieroglyph-like signs with Arabic letters. Some are recognisable Egyptian signs and many are not. Show a facsimile crop beside the true Egyptian sign and its modern value (from the Egyptian hall), marked agree or disagree only where a published comparison (El Daly 2005) supports it.
letters.note: 'high' grades the fact that the book has such tables (it is in Hammer's title), not any individual value. This is the unit at the centre of the El Daly debate (see claims). Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: Hieroglyphs read as signs for things and ideas
letters.form: CARD, NOTHING TO DRAW FROM THIS TEXT. Signs that the book explains by what they mean rather than how they sound. El Daly links this to the determinatives of Egyptian writing. Show the book's explanation beside the modern one, credited to El Daly.
letters.note: That the book treats some signs as symbols is El Daly's main point. Whether this is insight or the old Greek idea of symbolic hieroglyphs (as in Horapollo's Hieroglyphica) in a new setting is the heart of the dispute. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

lettersSource: NOT A SINGLE ALPHABET. The eight units are the kinds of script the Shawq lists, shown as cards. 'form' says what each card holds, and 'formConfidence' grades the card's facts (that the book has that kind of table), since nothing is described for drawing. No glyph is described: I saw no plate in this run, and drawing from memory would put invented letters under Ibn Waḥshiyya's name. Draw only from a public-domain scan of Hammer, Ancient Alphabets and Hieroglyphic Characters Explained (London, 1806), citing the page. Not from modern 'Ibn Wahshiyya' fonts or charts that give no page.

quotations.text: شوق المستهام في معرفة رموز الأقلام (Shawq al-mustahām fī maʿrifat rumūz al-aqlām)
quotations.translation: My own paraphrase, not a published translation: 'The longing of the love-crazed [seeker] to know the ciphers of the scripts'. (mustahām: one made distracted by love; rumūz: symbols, riddles, ciphers; aqlām: pens, hence scripts.) The brief's rendering, 'The book of the frenzied devotee's desire to learn the riddles of ancient scripts', could not be traced to a named translator in this run, so do not print it as anyone's translation.
quotations.source: Title of the work, as given in Hammer 1806 and in modern scholarship (Hämeen-Anttila 2006; El Daly 2005)

quotations.text: Ancient Alphabets and Hieroglyphic Characters Explained; with an Account of the Egyptian Priests, their Classes, Initiation, and Sacrifices
quotations.translation: Not a translation: Joseph Hammer's own English title (London: W. Bulmer and Co., 1806). Quoted from memory; check spelling and punctuation against a scan of the title page.

quotations.text: ثلاث عصي صففت بعد خاتم / على رأسها مثل السنان المقوم
quotations.translation: My own paraphrase: 'Three staffs set in a row after a seal [the star], with something like a straightened spear-point on their heads.' The Arabic is quoted from memory, and manuscripts and printings vary, so check it against a printed text before use. If it cannot be checked, print the paraphrase only.
quotations.source: Opening line of the poem on the seven seals (al-khawātim al-sabʿa), carried in the corpus under al-Būnī's name (Shams al-maʿārif). The ascription to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is traditional (legend). Not from the Shawq.

cautions: Every factual statement here rests on prior knowledge. The shared web-search budget ran out before this item began, so nothing was re-checked in this run. Treat dates and titles as needing one check against the named source before publication.
Never write 'Ibn Waḥshiyya deciphered the hieroglyphs'. Write 'El Daly argues that the book attributed to Ibn Waḥshiyya gives correct values for some signs', and give the objections.
Keep the ascription open: 'ascribed to Ibn Waḥshiyya' or 'the Shawq attributed to Ibn Waḥshiyya', since Hämeen-Anttila (2006) doubts it.

No glyph may be drawn from this file. Use only facsimile crops of Hammer 1806 (public domain), or tracings of them, with page references. Modern 'Ibn Wahshiyya alphabet' fonts and web charts are not sources.
'Nabataean' (Nabaṭī) in Ibn Waḥshiyya means the Aramaic-speaking people of Iraq, not the Nabataeans of Petra. Do not link to the Petra Nabataean script on that basis.

The Shawq is not the Picatrix (Ghāyat al-ḥakīm) and not al-Būnī's Shams al-maʿārif. The seven seals belong to the Būnian corpus and to talismanic practice; do not say the Shawq contains them unless a facsimile shows it.
Report the ascriptions of alphabets to Hermes, Plato and others as the book's (legend), and the poem of the seven seals' ascription to ʿAlī as tradition.
Hammer's title page gives the name as 'Ahmad Bin Abubekr Bin Wahshih', which garbles the usual Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Waḥshiyya. Quote it as Hammer prints it and explain the difference.
Do not repeat the story that Hammer's book helped Champollion unless a source is found. Champollion's 1822 decipherment rests on other evidence.
The seven seals are still used on amulets today. Describe them historically and neither endorse nor mock their use.
